newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: BP denies "dirty war" training to Colombian police.
newsitem.headline: BP denies "dirty war" training to Colombian police.

text.p: Oil giant British Petroleum Plc denied on Friday that it was training Colombian police with a "secret army" of former British Special Air Services (SAS) advisers.

The London-based Guardian newspaper and the World In Action TV program alleged last week that BP contracted the security service Defense Systems Colombia (DSC) to protect its oil rigs in eastern Colombia and provide "secret" police training, including counterinsurgency techniques and special weapons handling.

BP, like all oil companies in Colombia, have been declared military targets by the leftist National Liberation Army (ELN), the country's second largest rebel force set up by radical Roman Catholic priests in 1966.

"They (Defense Systems Colombia) don't train the police in any offensive actions or any kind of counterinsurgency techniques," Iain Conn, a vice chairman at BP's Colombian unit, told Reuters. "They do get involved in defensive tactics but it's not offensive training," he added.
Defense Systems Colombia, is a subsidiary of the London-based Defense Systems Limited -- a security force set up in 1981 by Alastair Morrison, an SAS hero and former No.2 of the elite fighting force.

John Doust, president of BP Exploration Colombia, said BP's contract with Defense Systems Colombia was not secret and said of the security firm's 120 employees working for the oil-giant in Colombia just six were former SAS members.
"They provide advice on how to protect an oil installation and discuss those kinds of things with the police and they may get involved with defensive positioning," Doust added.
A spokesman for Defense Systems Colombia said about 60 percent of 300 Colombia-based staff were former military personnel but said only about 20 men were foreigners.
He said the company "emphatically" rejected links to groups of mercenaries and said its worldwide clients included the World Bank, the United Nations and the International Committee of the Red Cross.

The SAS has a long history of involvement with Colombia's armed forces and is credited with training counternarcotics units, elite anti-kidnap or GAULA squads and most recently helped form a rapid response anti-guerrilla force in Bogota, according to police chiefs.
